title: TreeSet and LinkedHashSet
learningObjectives: Store unique elements in sorted order with TreeSet
Preserve insertion order while enforcing uniqueness with LinkedHashSet
Explain how natural ordering and comparators control TreeSet order
Demonstrate how comparator equality affects set uniqueness
Select a set implementation based on ordering requirements

understand.concept: TreeSet stores unique elements in sorted order. LinkedHashSet preserves insertion order. A comparator that returns zero treats values as duplicates in a TreeSet.
understand.whyItMatters: TreeSet and LinkedHashSet helps learners create Java applications that are easier to reason about, test and maintain.
understand.analogy: Treat the concept as a clearly labeled tool for one programming responsibility.
understand.analogyLimit: Actual behavior is defined by Java language rules and API contracts.

explain.narrative:
## Set contracts and ordering choices

A Set stores no duplicate elements according to its equality rule. The Set interface describes uniqueness but does not promise a particular iteration order. Choose an implementation based on the ordering contract the application needs.

## HashSet, LinkedHashSet and TreeSet

- HashSet uses hashing and makes no iteration-order guarantee. Its typical membership operations are efficient when hash codes are well distributed.
- LinkedHashSet maintains insertion encounter order while enforcing uniqueness. It is useful when output should follow the order in which distinct values were first added.
- TreeSet keeps elements sorted by natural ordering or a supplied Comparator. Its basic add, remove and contains operations are logarithmic-time in the documented balanced-tree implementation.

## Comparator equality controls uniqueness

TreeSet uses its ordering comparison to decide whether two elements occupy the same set position. If compare(a, b) returns zero, the set treats the values as equivalent for set membership, even if a.equals(b) is false. Design comparators carefully and make their ordering consistent with equals when practical.

## Nulls and type requirements

HashSet and LinkedHashSet permit a null element. TreeSet generally cannot compare null with its natural-order elements; a custom comparator must explicitly define null handling if null is to be supported. Elements in a TreeSet must be mutually comparable under the selected ordering.

## Practical selection

Use HashSet for uniqueness without order requirements, LinkedHashSet for uniqueness plus insertion order, and TreeSet for uniqueness plus sorted traversal. Declare variables using Set<E> when callers need only the interface contract. Do not write tests that expect HashSet iteration order.

examples.title: Core API
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Set<Integer> values = new java.util.TreeSet<>(java.util.List.of(3,1,2)); System.out.println(values); } }
examples.explanation: TreeSet orders the inserted values by their natural ordering and removes duplicate values according to its comparison result.

examples.title: Practical use
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Set<String> values = new java.util.LinkedHashSet<>(); values.add("B"); values.add("A"); values.add("B"); System.out.println(values); } }
examples.explanation: LinkedHashSet rejects the repeated value but iterates the remaining elements in their insertion order.

examples.title: Boundary behavior
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Set<Integer> values = new java.util.TreeSet<>(); values.add(5); values.add(5); System.out.println(values.size()); } }
examples.explanation: The contains call checks membership using the set's equality and hashing contract; the boolean result is printed explicitly.

examples.title: Alternative pattern
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Set<String> values = new java.util.TreeSet<>(java.util.Comparator.reverseOrder()); values.add("A"); values.add("C"); values.add("B"); System.out.println(values); } }
examples.explanation: Comparator.reverseOrder supplies descending natural order, so TreeSet iterates from the greatest value to the least.

examples.title: Verify the result
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println(new java.util.TreeSet<>(java.util.List.of("pear","apple","orange"))); } }
examples.explanation: The default String ordering is lexicographic and case-sensitive; values whose comparison is zero are considered duplicates by TreeSet.

practise.guidedTask: Insert duplicate and unsorted values into a TreeSet and LinkedHashSet. Print both and explain their different iteration orders.
practise.independentTask: Use a Comparator to sort strings in reverse order with TreeSet. Explain how compare returning zero affects uniqueness.
hints: Use HashSet when no iteration order is required, LinkedHashSet for insertion order, and TreeSet for sorted order.
For TreeSet, inspect Comparator.compare: a zero result means the set regards the elements as equivalent.
Do not assume HashSet iteration order; test membership and size instead.
practise.challenge: Create a case-insensitive TreeSet of names and test values that differ only by letter case; explain why one may be treated as equivalent.

questions.prompt: Which set implementation maintains elements in sorted order?
questions.explanation: TreeSet uses natural ordering here, so the integers are traversed in ascending order and duplicate comparison-equal values are stored once.

questions.prompt: Which set implementation preserves insertion order?
questions.explanation: LinkedHashSet preserves insertion encounter order while enforcing set uniqueness; the second B does not create another element.

questions.prompt: What does a TreeSet use to determine sorted order?
options: The order of source file declarations
questions.explanation: The two inserted integers compare equal, so Set membership retains one distinct value and size is one.

questions.prompt: If a TreeSet comparator returns zero for two values, what happens?
options: The set treats them as equivalent for uniqueness
questions.answer: The set treats them as equivalent for uniqueness
questions.explanation: Comparator.reverseOrder reverses the natural String order, producing C before B before A.

questions.prompt: When is LinkedHashSet a good choice?
options: When uniqueness and predictable insertion order are both needed
When duplicate values must be preserved
questions.answer: When uniqueness and predictable insertion order are both needed
questions.explanation: TreeSet traverses String keys in their natural lexicographic order; comparison equality determines whether a new value is distinct.
